newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Zedillo sees Jan-Aug inflation 18.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Zedillo sees Jan-Aug inflation 18.5 pct.

text.p: Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo said on Sunday that inflation in the first eight months of the year would be around 18.5 percent, and he projected economic growth next year of at least four percent.

In his second State of the Nation address, Zedillo declared Mexico's economic "emergency" over, and said the economy was clearly back on the road to recovery, though he acknowledged that growth remained insufficient.

Inflation, he said, was on the way down. "Between January and August 1995, price levels increased 38 percent. It is estimated that the increase this year in the same period will be around 18.5 percent," he said.
In the January-July period, the consumer price index rose an accumulated 16.94 percent, and it was up 0.71 percent in the first half of August.

Next year's budget would seek to curb inflation further while targetting growth rates of at least four percent, and also will include retaining the current free floating exchange rate system and fiscal and monetary discipline, Zedillo said.

"I will propose a strategy for 1997 that will allow a growth rate of gross domestic product of at least four percent, (and) that will favor a further reduction in inflation and interest rates," he said.
Next year's budget, he pledged, would maintain "fiscal and monetary discipline and the free-floating exchange rate."
He said his plans for the future included growth above four percent per year starting in 1998, and he outlined what he called three "essential tasks" going forward:
-- Continued application of the economic program that has brought Mexico out of crisis;
-- Continued structural reforms that improve the economy's efficiency;
-- Increased national savings so that investment can increase without risks of the sort of crises that have plagued Mexico in the past 20 years.

Zedillo said one of the cornerstones of his plan for sustained economic growth was social security reform, in which starting next year private pension funds will be given the green light to handle and invest workers' savings.
"I am fully convinced that because of its positive effect on long-term domestic savings, the reform of the pension system will be what most contributes to sustained growth in our economy," he said.

In the immediate future, however, he said private investment, exports and a gradual recovery in consumption would be the motors of growth in 1997, with special emphasis on privatizations and liberalization of railways, telecommunications, and power plants.
Public funding would be chiefly directed at emergency programs such as debt support efforts channelled via the banking sector.
The cost of that support on the public coffers would be about 180 billion pesos at constant 1996 prices over coming years, he said.
